10037024.notes: Paper states neutron pulses of ~1.5 ns duration (FWHM). Samples were placed 10 cm from the neutron source; main detector distance varied from 220 to 310 cm, so scatter->detector stored as midpoint 2.65±0.45 m and total TOF path (source->scatter + scatter->detector) as 2.75±0.45 m. Data reduction used a Monte Carlo correction that included time-of-flight resolution; detector/electronics timing contributions beyond pulse width are not explicitly quoted, so Δt=1.5 ns should be treated as a lower-bound input.

10571002.notes: ORELA TOF reported as a 40 m flight path with incident spectrum resolution 0.2 ns/m (treated as an effective timing term already including source/moderator/instrument contributions). Thus Δt_eff = (0.2 ns/m)*40 m = 8 ns. EXFOR text also describes scattering geometry with 5 m source->scatterer and 5 m scatterer->detector legs; those lengths describe the scattering setup, but the incident neutron energy resolution used here is tied to the 40 m TOF station. Data were averaged over 100 keV incident-energy bins, so practical incident-energy resolution is not better than the bin width even if TOF allows finer resolution.

notes: EXFOR 11276 (COO-1573-33, 1967) specifies TOF method but does not provide flight-path distances or timing resolution in the BIB information available here.

A closely related Case Western Reserve (1USACSE) TOF scattering setup is documented in EXFOR 10037 (Boschung/Lindow/Shrader, Nucl. Phys. A161 (1971)), using a 3-MeV terminal pulsed Van de Graaff with Mobley magnet beam buncher, D(d,n) source, and liquid scintillator with pulse-shape discrimination. This may indicate similar instrumentation family, but distances/timing must still be taken from the 1967 report or derived from peak widths/energy spread.

If the 1967 report (COO-1573-33) can be accessed, extract the actual source→scatterer and scatterer→detector distances and the effective timing resolution (beam pulse width/bunch width + detector timing + electronics) and fill the null values above.

14462002.notes: TOF used with a pulsed/bunched beam; bunch width about 1 ns (used here as timing input). Detector mounted on a goniometer; paper states it can accommodate a flight path up to 4 m but does not give the exact flight path used for the reported datasets, so distance=4 m is an upper bound assumption. Actual flight path may be <4 m, which would worsen TOF energy resolution. Timing contributions from detector/electronics (beyond beam bunch width) are not explicitly given, so the true effective Δt is likely >1 ns.

20743002.notes: Assumed that Karlsruhe ISO-CYCLO TOF spectrometer used an evacuated flight path of ~57 m for neutron timing measurements (there is a longer flight path of 195m, information is not clear which one was used). EXFOR indicates a neutron pulse width of 2 ns and an instrument timing term of 0.09 ns/m; interpreted as separate timing contributions. Using L = 57 m gives spectrometer timing = 0.09 ns/m * 57 = 5.13 ns. Combined in quadrature with the 2 ns pulse width yields Δt_eff ≈ 5.47 ns for conservative time resolution.
